keptItems.title: ‘Nothing About This Was Inevitable’
keptItems.summaryEvidence: The second floor of OpenAI’s old headquarters had a theme. Each room was named after one of the most important inventions in human history: “Clock,” “Fire,” and, of course, “AGI,” or artificial general intelligence. I saw this in the spring of 2024, when I was interviewing some of the company’s researchers about recent technical advances . At the time, ChatGPT was still making embarrassing arithmetic errors, and the notion that the bot would ever rival human intelligence was dubious. But here, in the renovated shell of a former mayonnaise factory in San Francisco, AGI’s arrival was predestined. This belief in AGI—a computer program with capabilities that rival or even exceed those of the human mind—is foundational to the mission of Google DeepMind, OpenAI, and Anthropic, three of the most influential AI companies in the world. And the pursuit of that milestone is the subject of The AGI Chronicles , a new book by the tech reporter and Atlantic contributing writer Kevin Roose, which he describes as his attempt to document the decade “when the human monopoly on advanced intelligence ended, and a new world was born.” Roose, a prominent and well-connected commenter on the AI boom, follows the internecine world of the frontier AI companies in remarkable, at times almost insular, detail. Based on interviews with more than 150 researchers, executives, investors, and policy makers close to the technology’s development, The AGI Chronicles traces crucial moments across DeepMind, OpenAI, and Anthropic from 2015 through early 2026 to figure out how we got to this very messy moment in AI

keptItems.title: Anne Carson’s Seductive Strangeness
keptItems.summaryEvidence: Anne Carson, who won the 2026 Nobel Prize in Literature today, doesn’t write masterpieces or door-stoppers, and she has no interest in emulating the great works of the past—including those of past laureates. Despite her training as a classicist and her celebrated skill as a translator, she would likely have little to say about the authenticity of film adaptations of The Odyssey . Carson is a poet by trade, but she’s really an archaeologist of sorts, sifting through the pottery shards of culture and letting the light of our own time illuminate their beauty. Carson prefers to use fragments as seeds for her own poetry, and the high-cultural touchpoints for her lyrics and critical essays—Sappho, Samuel Beckett, Franz Kafka, Michelangelo Antonioni, Simone Weil—sometimes give her work an air of forbidding experimentation that quickly turns, upon reading, into pleasure and delight. You may not know or care who Heloïse and Abelard are, but I can promise that you will enjoy reading them argue in a hotel room in the middle of her 2005 “spoken-word opera,” Decreation . Across roughly two dozen translations and original books, a twee-punk “don’t give a damn” attitude pervades Carson’s reinterpretation of ancient texts: Her poetry shuns obeisance to tradition and literality and embraces creative fantasy instead. For that reason, the barrier to entry for her poetry is surprisingly low—surprisingly, I mean, for a poet whose books often contain a page or two of footnotes. keptItems.title: The Oil Crisis America Saw Coming
keptItems.summaryEvidence: This is an edition of Time-Travel Thursdays, a journey through The Atlantic ’s archives to contextualize the present. Sign up here. In December 1987, The Atlantic had some reassuring news for readers: The next oil crisis didn’t have to happen. The United States had already endured the oil shocks of the 1970s, and Amory B. Lovins and L. Hunter Lovins, a pair of then-married environmentalists, argued in this magazine that the country had learned from the experience. The U.S. had diversified its sources of foreign oil, and the American economy needed less oil to grow, a shift that the Lovinses attributed mainly to efficiency gains, such as better-insulated buildings and more fuel-efficient cars. Oil production had grown outside OPEC, an organization of oil-exporting states, reducing the world’s reliance on Persian Gulf oil. Even the Strait of Hormuz, a flash point in the Iran-Iraq War of the ’80s, appeared less threatening to the global supply. By 1987, less oil was passing through the waterway than earlier in the decade, and the Lovinses believed that reserves and alternative routes could help make up for any sudden cutoffs caused by geopolitical tensions. The moment offered what the writers called a “unique opportunity”: a reprieve from Middle Eastern dominance of the global oil supply. “If this interval is frittered away,” they warned, “it could end with the United States, its alternative options expired, needing Middle Eastern oil more than ever.” Nearly four decades later, America is far less vulnerable to foreign-oil disruptions, but it is once again caught in a global o

keptItems.title: What I Saw at New York’s Anti-Israel October 7 Rallies
keptItems.summaryEvidence: Yesterday was a reminder of the difficulty that the pro-Palestine left has with showing grace even for the dead. On the third anniversary of the day that Hamas gunmen and freelance killers arrived in Israel on motorcycles and paragliders and trucks, and slaughtered children and grandparents and mothers and fathers and dancing young people, New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani put out a statement that was empathetic and modulated in tone … for about 50 words. “This day is profoundly painful for so many New Yorkers,” Mamdani began. “It marks three years since the horrific war crimes of October 7. On that day, Hamas killed more than 1,100 Israelis and abducted 251 others. We grieve alongside our many friends and neighbors who still carry that unthinkable loss.” Alas, then came the next 162 words, as the young mayor indulged his anger with Israel. He apparently felt obligated to give New York City—which is home to the biggest Jewish population of any city on the globe—a history lesson that seemed to suggest that Israel brought the October 7 tragedy upon itself. “The suffering did not begin nor end that day,” he wrote. “It instead continued through the Israeli government’s devastating, ongoing genocide in Gaza, in which it has killed more than 74,000 Palestinians—including more than 21,000 children. manifest.title: ASEAN’s Economic Future in an Age of Geoeconomic Competition
manifest.summaryEvidence: Over the past two decades, since the ASEAN Economic Community was envisioned, ASEAN has benefited from an increasingly open global economy. Its strategy of remaining open to all major economies, attracting investment, integrating into global supply chains and avoiding choosing sides has served the region well, but this model is now under pressure. The intensifying US-China strategic rivalry and tariff wars, export controls and competition over semiconductors and critical minerals are reshaping the global economic landscape.

manifest.title: ‘Nothing About This Was Inevitable’
manifest.summaryEvidence: The second floor of OpenAI’s old headquarters had a theme. Each room was named after one of the most important inventions in human history: “Clock,” “Fire,” and, of course, “AGI,” or artificial general intelligence. I saw this in the spring of 2024, when I was interviewing some of the company’s researchers about recent technical advances . At the time, ChatGPT was still making embarrassing arithmetic errors, and the notion that the bot would ever rival human intelligence was dubious. But here, in the renovated shell of a former mayonnaise factory in San Francisco, AGI’s arrival was predestined. This belief in AGI—a computer program with capabilities that rival or even exceed those of the human mind—is foundational to the mission of Google DeepMind, OpenAI, and Anthropic, three of the most influential AI companies in the world. And the pursuit of that milestone is the subject of The AGI Chronicles , a new book by the tech reporter and Atlantic contributing writer Kevin Roose, which he describes as his attempt to document the decade “when the human monopoly on advanced intelligence ended, and a new world was born.” Roose, a prominent and well-connected commenter on the AI boom, follows the internecine world of the frontier AI companies in remarkable, at times almost insular, detail. Based on interviews with more than 150 researchers, executives, investors, and policy makers close to the technology’s development, The AGI Chronicles traces crucial moments across DeepMind, OpenAI, and Anthropic from 2015 through early 2026 to figure out how we got to this very messy moment in AI

manifest.title: Anne Carson’s Seductive Strangeness
manifest.summaryEvidence: Anne Carson, who won the 2026 Nobel Prize in Literature today, doesn’t write masterpieces or door-stoppers, and she has no interest in emulating the great works of the past—including those of past laureates. Despite her training as a classicist and her celebrated skill as a translator, she would likely have little to say about the authenticity of film adaptations of The Odyssey . Carson is a poet by trade, but she’s really an archaeologist of sorts, sifting through the pottery shards of culture and letting the light of our own time illuminate their beauty. Carson prefers to use fragments as seeds for her own poetry, and the high-cultural touchpoints for her lyrics and critical essays—Sappho, Samuel Beckett, Franz Kafka, Michelangelo Antonioni, Simone Weil—sometimes give her work an air of forbidding experimentation that quickly turns, upon reading, into pleasure and delight. You may not know or care who Heloïse and Abelard are, but I can promise that you will enjoy reading them argue in a hotel room in the middle of her 2005 “spoken-word opera,” Decreation . Across roughly two dozen translations and original books, a twee-punk “don’t give a damn” attitude pervades Carson’s reinterpretation of ancient texts: Her poetry shuns obeisance to tradition and literality and embraces creative fantasy instead. For that reason, the barrier to entry for her poetry is surprisingly low—surprisingly, I mean, for a poet whose books often contain a page or two of footnotes. manifest.title: The Oil Crisis America Saw Coming
manifest.summaryEvidence: This is an edition of Time-Travel Thursdays, a journey through The Atlantic ’s archives to contextualize the present. Sign up here. In December 1987, The Atlantic had some reassuring news for readers: The next oil crisis didn’t have to happen. The United States had already endured the oil shocks of the 1970s, and Amory B. Lovins and L. Hunter Lovins, a pair of then-married environmentalists, argued in this magazine that the country had learned from the experience. The U.S. had diversified its sources of foreign oil, and the American economy needed less oil to grow, a shift that the Lovinses attributed mainly to efficiency gains, such as better-insulated buildings and more fuel-efficient cars. Oil production had grown outside OPEC, an organization of oil-exporting states, reducing the world’s reliance on Persian Gulf oil. Even the Strait of Hormuz, a flash point in the Iran-Iraq War of the ’80s, appeared less threatening to the global supply. By 1987, less oil was passing through the waterway than earlier in the decade, and the Lovinses believed that reserves and alternative routes could help make up for any sudden cutoffs caused by geopolitical tensions. manifest.summaryEvidence: Yesterday was a reminder of the difficulty that the pro-Palestine left has with showing grace even for the dead. On the third anniversary of the day that Hamas gunmen and freelance killers arrived in Israel on motorcycles and paragliders and trucks, and slaughtered children and grandparents and mothers and fathers and dancing young people, New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani put out a statement that was empathetic and modulated in tone … for about 50 words. “This day is profoundly painful for so many New Yorkers,” Mamdani began. “It marks three years since the horrific war crimes of October 7. On that day, Hamas killed more than 1,100 Israelis and abducted 251 others. We grieve alongside our many friends and neighbors who still carry that unthinkable loss.” Alas, then came the next 162 words, as the young mayor indulged his anger with Israel. He apparently felt obligated to give New York City—which is home to the biggest Jewish population of any city on the globe—a history lesson that seemed to suggest that Israel brought the October 7 tragedy upon itself. “The suffering did not begin nor end that day,” he wrote. “It instead continued through the Israeli government’s devastating, ongoing genocide in Gaza, in which it has killed more than 74,000 Palestinians—including more than 21,000 children.
